deep_dive.title: Standardized Tolerance for Adaptive Reuse and Repair: A Method for HNSW Migration Under Embedding Model Change Scenarios
deep_dive.abstract: When an embedding model changes, the same collection is re-encoded, and its vector index must be adapted to the new embedding space. Because the source and target vectors represent the same objects, suitable connections in the source index can be reused. We propose STARR (Standardized Tolerance for Adaptive Reuse and Repair) to migrate HNSW indexes after an embedding model change. STARR compares standardized edge lengths over the same source neighbor lists in both embedding spaces and uses the correlation between their distance profiles to set the allowable increase in standardized edge length. It reconnects affected vertices by searching the partially migrated graph and shares the resulting candidates with their neighbors. We bound edge rejection under local distance distortion, characterize migration work, and prove that a final repair pass makes every vertex reachable from the entry point at the base layer while respecting degree limits. Single-threaded experiments on MS MARCO, Wikipedia, and CC3M, each with one million objects, show that STARR achieves 5.25--44.54$\times$ construction speedups over Fresh and migrates faster than both DGM variants on all 15 selected transitions. Recall@10 remains within one percentage point of Fresh in 10 cases, and query throughput exceeds DGM-Local in 14 cases. Parameter sweeps on three transitions further demonstrate favorable migration-time--recall tradeoffs beyond the default settings. Across all 240 directed transitions among 16 MS MARCO models, STARR achieves a median construction speedup of 16.71$\times$ with a median recall loss of 1.0 percentage point.

deep_dive.title: Look Before You Leap: Re-Architecting Disk-Resident Vector Search with TriVS
deep_dive.abstract: Disk-resident approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) scales vector search beyond DRAM, yet state-of-the-art systems remain I/O-bound, even with fast SSDs and sophisticated I/O execution. To understand this bottleneck, we conduct an I/O-centric analysis that breaks each query down into an approach phase that locates a query-near region and a converge phase that resolves the final top-k. This analysis reveals complementary I/O tradeoffs: cluster-based search circumvents approach-phase I/O through in-memory routing but reads coarse-grained, full clusters during convergence, whereas graph-based search employs fine-grained, vector-level I/O throughout, enabling efficient convergence at the cost of inevitable I/O during the approach phase.   To combine the complementary I/O benefits of the two granularities, we present TriVS, a new paradigm that re-architects disk-resident vector search as a trilogy: approach coarsely, distill progressively, and converge exactly. Its key innovations come in two parts. First, it decouples the approach and converge phases from a single search granularity, employing cluster-based search to avoid approach-phase I/O and leveraging vector-level I/O for efficient convergence. Second, to bridge the two granularities, it introduces a new in-memory distill phase between the original two, progressively reducing routed clusters to a vector-level shortlist using compact quantized vectors before disk access. Moreover, coarser clustering shrinks the centroid-routing index, allowing TriVS to reallocate existing memory to distillation rather than expand its memory budget. Our evaluation on five datasets spanning diverse vector types and scales shows that, at Recall@10=0.9, TriVS achieves on average 3.42X PipeANN's throughput, 51.2% lower latency, and 63.7% less disk I/O, while using less memory and storage than PipeANN.

deep_dive.title: LEDGER: Auditable Agent Memory Under Change
deep_dive.abstract: Agent memory systems are mostly evaluated on fixed histories, and only their final answers are scored. In real use, facts change, sources differ in reliability, and users ask the agent to forget things. We present LEDGER, a memory layer in which a language model proposes facts and explicit rules decide which value is current, which source to trust, and what to delete. Each fact keeps its source and the period in which it held. LEDGER+EP adds a search over raw conversation turns for questions the ledger does not cover, and scrubs these turns on deletion. We compare both against no memory, full-history replay, retrieval over raw transcripts, and Mem0, with the same answering model and prompt, on a synthetic multi-session coding-agent workload and a 210-question subset of LongMemEval, and we score both the evidence each memory sends to the model and the answer. On the coding workload, LEDGER+EP in fallback mode answers 94.3% of questions correctly on five development seeds and 91.1% on five held-out seeds, against 82.1% and 83.3% for full replay, the strongest baseline. When a deletion request only describes the fact, no deleted value reached our systems' evidence in any evaluated probe. On LongMemEval, LEDGER+EP in augment mode has the same observed accuracy as full replay (74.8%) with 1% of its context. The main limitation is that the coding workload is synthetic and built by us; on LongMemEval, the differences between the strongest systems are within the confidence intervals.

deep_dive.title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
deep_dive.abstract: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.

deep_dive.title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
deep_dive.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

deep_dive.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
deep_dive.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. It treats indexing and orchestration as first-class components and agentic workflows as a paradigm of their own, and it covers the agentic work that has appeared since those reviews. Beyond these components, it covers evaluation, applications, and the questions that remain open for future exploration. From tradition to present and beyond, this work systematically reviews RAG from a perspective of the agentic era.

deep_dive.title: Composing Independently Distilled Memory and Retrieval Policies for Long-Term Agents
deep_dive.abstract: Long-lived Web assistants require effective memory and retrieval mechanisms to access information from past user interactions. While these capabilities can be learned through specialized policies, it remains unclear whether specialists trained independently in different environments can be effectively composed without joint optimization. This paper investigates compositional transfer through policy distillation. Memory-writing and sequential retrieval policies are independently distilled from frontier-model action trajectories into 3B models and combined with a fixed answer generator without downstream training. On a LongMemEval-based benchmark, the distilled composition achieves 73.1% accuracy, compared with 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms the evaluated RL-trained compositions on PersonaMem-v2. Component ablations reveal that improvements in individual policies depend on their composition, highlighting the importance of cross-specialist compatibility. Further task-specific adaptation improves accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval through RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 through supervised distillation. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of independent specialist distillation for modular multi-agent systems. Source code and datasets of teacher-generated memory-editing and retrieval trajectories are released to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

quick_skim.title: Lost in the Hallway: Benchmarking Persistent Spatial Memory Across Revisits
quick_skim.abstract: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.

quick_skim.title: When the Bill Falls: Reusing the Old Index Defers,Never Avoids, Re-encoding in Complete Embedding-Model Migration
quick_skim.abstract: Upgrading the embedding model behind a vector index requires re-encoding the corpus. Recent work reuses the old index through adapters or window re-ranking. Across sixteen model pairs on passage and code corpora, plus eleven on Natural Questions (NQ), we find three results. First, reuse never avoids re-encoding: if migration must complete, every strategy eventually encodes every document; reuse only changes when that work is paid and the quality served meanwhile. Second, adapters should be compared with the old model, not only the new one. Of five adapter variants, only same-family LLM bridges beat the old model, and only by a negligible margin. Third, window re-ranking cost can be priced from the old index alone; pre-registered replays on all 8,841,823 passages confirmed the prediction on all three tested pairs. Workload skew also matters: across 36 further pre-registered Zipf replays, the planned family matched on 32. These findings yield three pre-migration rules: whether reuse is worthwhile, which strategy to use, and how deep a window to take. The depth rule priced every window that reached target quality to within 4 parts in 10^5 of the corpus. On NQ, a pre-committed plan selected the family on 10 of 11 pairs and priced every window exactly. Quality inputs transferred less reliably across corpus scale, so the model gap and window quality loss must be measured on the serving index.

quick_skim.title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
quick_skim.abstract: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

quick_skim.title: MemMend: A Selective Revision Framework for Memory Question Answering
quick_skim.abstract: Revising every answer from a long-term memory can consume substantial inference budget and damage facts that were already correct. We introduce MemMend, a modular selective revision framework that routes potentially incomplete answers to an editor, represents corrections as bounded exact-text replacements, and accepts only edits with resolvable source coordinates and valid edit operations. The editor preserves the current answer when no legal repair is proposed; accepted edits require no additional semantic-verification call. On 1,986 LoCoMo development questions, MemMend achieves 67.17 conversation-macro F1 and 88.35 mean Judge score, improving over a verified revision chain by 0.82 and 1.24 points while using 62.37% fewer revision calls. Routing uses 54.15% fewer revision calls than ungated local review, with similar F1 but a 0.67-point lower Judge score. Applied directly to native PropMem, Mem0, and SimpleMem answers, the editing interface raises F1 by 3.79, 6.44, and 0.42 points. It outperforms same-gate rewriting and saves 49.85-83.72% of editing calls relative to ungated editing, which retains higher F1 in this adaptation. A source-by-editing factorial supports local editing for F1 but leaves an independent quality benefit from source obligations unresolved. Transfer to 451 LongMemEval-V2 Small questions also favors revision efficiency, while an external PerLTQA dialogue subset reveals a completeness gap. These results support selective editing as a reusable quality-cost operating point.

quick_skim.title: The abc index: Exact Retrieval for Learned Sparse Representations
quick_skim.abstract: In learned sparse retrieval (LSR), queries have tens of terms with learned weights, on which classic dynamic pruning is believed to fail, and approximate indexes such as Seismic and HNSW are considered faster than exact ones. We challenge this view with abc, an exact index built only from standard IR techniques: term-at-a-time (TAAT) evaluation, Block-Max MaxScore, binary packing and doc-id reordering. They are combined in a new design and engineered for modern CPUs. On MS MARCO encoded with four LSR models, the abc index is the fastest exact index at every k: 6.5-84x faster than the exact search of Qdrant, 13-55x faster than that of Lucene, and 2.9-18x faster than BMP with an index 5-7x smaller. Against approximate indexes, it takes 1.5-3.6x less space, and its latency grows much more slowly with k: they are up to 4.3x faster at k=10, but at k=1000 it overtakes them, by up to 7.4x. Exactness comes with an extra benefit: there are no parameters to tune.

quick_skim.title: When Visually Rich Documents Meet Multi-Vector Retrieval for Region-level Retrieval-Augmented Generation
quick_skim.abstract: Visually rich documents (VRDs) convey knowledge through textual, visual, and layout information that text-centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Text-RAG) struggles to fully exploit. Recent Vision-RAG approaches enable retrieval and generation directly from document images, retaining this multimodal information. However, earlier Vision-RAG methods commonly adopt coarse retrieval representations and full-page visual contexts, which can obscure local evidence and introduce substantial redundancy and computational overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MV-VisRAG, a region-level Vision-RAG framework that uses semantically complete regions for both document representation and visual augmentation. Specifically, MV-VisRAG first constructs these regions through a ContentAdaptive Regionalization module. It then encodes them into local region vectors and a page-level global vector using a VLM-based retriever trained through multimodal reconstruction pretraining and retrieval fine-tuning. With this compact multi-vector representation, MV-VisRAG performs late-interaction retrieval and estimates region contributions from the resulting matching scores. These contributions guide the selection of relevant regions, which are then rearranged into a compact visual context for generation. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate retrieval and generation gains over corresponding baselines, while region-level augmentation substantially reduces visual tokens and computational cost. Our code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xandery-geek/MV-VisRAG.

quick_skim.title: Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?
quick_skim.abstract: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

quick_skim.title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
quick_skim.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

quick_skim.title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
quick_skim.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.

quick_skim.title: VistaTree: Question Answering over Long Multimodal Documents with Image-Derived Summary Trees
quick_skim.abstract: Answering questions over long multimodal documents requires locating relevant evidence across pages containing text, tables, and figures. When the document exceeds the model's context window, selective retrieval becomes necessary. We introduce VistaTree, a document question-answering agent that builds a summary tree directly from rendered page images. VistaTree segments documents into contiguous page spans, recursively groups them into a topic hierarchy, and refines sibling summaries to distinguish neighboring sections. At query time, the agent uses node summaries to select relevant nodes and reads the corresponding pages, using hierarchical navigation when the full outline exceeds the context budget. Experiments on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL evaluate answer quality and retrieval cost using a locally hosted vision-language model, and quantify the performance gap between global and hierarchical access to the index.

quick_skim.title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
quick_skim.abstract: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.

quick_skim.title: FORGETMENOT: Auditing Memory Driven Privacy Risks in Commercial AI Agents
quick_skim.abstract: Commercial AI agents increasingly incorporate long-term memory (both persistent and chat-history) to enable more accurate and personalized responses, raises significant privacy and policy concerns. Yet little is known about user privacy risks associated with memory behavior, in particular, about memory storage, disclosure, transparency and deletion control. To bridge this gap, we propose FORGETMENOT, an auditing framework for analyzing the privacy risks of long term memory in commercial AI agents. Using our framework, we collect around 3800 multi-turn sessions comprising around 6M tokens across five popular AI agents. Our results show that agents store a wide range of personal attributes, including demographics, health, and sensitive details. Furthermore, user visible memory reveals substantially less (around 20% on average) attributes than the agents store in practice, exposing a significant transparency gap. Our stealth memory injection (SMI) technique further increases the amount of personal and sensitive attribute stored in memory, raising it by 25% and 15% for Copilot and Claude, respectively. We further observed memory deletion control is unreliable, as all five agents exhibit non-zero post deletion leakage, including health and self-harm related attributes. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of memory disclosure to a 3rd-party email recipient as a proof-of-concept, as Gemini shows 31.9% leakage rate. Together, our findings reveal notable privacy risks in commercial agents memory. Finally, we discuss both design implications and regulatory recommendations to protect users memory privacy in commercial agents.

quick_skim.title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
quick_skim.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.

quick_skim.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
quick_skim.abstract: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.
